turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Come on through, the pair of you. I've the repeat list from the chemist pulled up, whenever you're ready.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): How are you keeping at all? Sit in, there's no rush. What's been on your mind?
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): I'm grand. Honestly. I'm only in for the same script, doctor, nothing exciting.
[SEG0004] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He's not grand, I'll say it straight. I'm Nuala, I do the mornings. He's sore and he makes little of it.
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): Ah Nuala, would you give over. It's a niggle. People have worse.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): A niggle where, though? Start wherever you like.

[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): It's the left knee. Well, actually I thought the hip for a day, and then no, it's the knee. Aches a small bit, only a couple of weeks. Walking to the shop is the worst of it, and sitting down eases it.
[SEG0008] person_4 (CAREGIVER): A couple of weeks? It's been three months, doctor. He stops halfway up the lane. He just won't say that.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Does that pain wake you in the night?
[SEG0010] person_3 (PATIENT): Not at all. I sleep like a log, so I do.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any swelling in it, or does it feel hot to you?
[SEG0012] person_3 (PATIENT): No swelling. And it's not hot. I'm not imagining things.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): What about heartburn, with the anti-inflammatory tablets?
[SEG0014] person_3 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, I won't mark that down as a yes. You're hoping for a stronger painkiller, am I right?
[SEG0016] person_3 (PATIENT): If you've something better I'll take it. Your man next door is on tramadol and he's out with the dog morning and night. I'd take that yoke.
[SEG0017] person_4 (CAREGIVER): The neighbour's tramadol is the neighbour's business. And your sister's biotin for her nails, that's her own tablets, don't be bringing those into it.
[SEG0018] person_3 (PATIENT): My brother Tommy is the one on metformin, for his diabetes. He tried giving me a lecture. I don't want his tablets.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): We won't be using Tommy's tablets, or the neighbour's. Let me think this out loud for a second.

[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): It could be osteoarthritis grumbling in the left knee, or it could be a bit of bursitis along the side. I'm not putting one label on it today, and I'm not concluding you need a stronger painkiller.
[SEG0021] person_3 (PATIENT): So that's a no on the tramadol.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's a no. No tramadol, and no codeine either. You'd only be drowsy and constipated, and the knee would be much the same.
[SEG0023] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He has a biscuit tin full of boxes as it is. We nearly missed the bus, the 11 was late again, but sure.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): The bus is a menace these days. Let's go through your own tablets, nice and slow. Ramipril five milligrams in the morning, that's for the high blood pressure?
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): That's the one, yeah.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): And are you getting it in every morning, or does it slip?
[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): Ah, I suppose. Most mornings. If I'm late for the post office I leave it in the blister.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's worth knowing, thank you. Atorvastatin twenty milligrams at night, for the cholesterol?
[SEG0029] person_3 (PATIENT): Every night, with the tea. I don't miss that one.
[SEG0030] person_1 (NURSE): Paracetamol on the list is one gram four times a day. Is that what you swallow?
[SEG0031] person_3 (PATIENT): Two of the five-hundred tablets, four times a day. Yeah. Doesn't do a whole lot, if I'm honest.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stay at that and don't go over it, and take them regular rather than waiting until you're hobbling. Now, the naproxen.
[SEG0033] person_1 (NURSE): The pharmacy list has naproxen two hundred and fifty milligrams, twice a day.
[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): No, that's wrong. I take five hundred milligrams, twice a day. They've the strength mixed up.
[SEG0035] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I saw a box in the press. Um, I thought maybe the two-fifty, but he says five hundred. I wouldn't bet the house on it.

[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Then we don't guess. What's on the list and what you're telling me don't match, so I'm not writing a strength down until we see the box. You do both have it as twice a day, with food?
[SEG0037] person_3 (PATIENT): Twice a day, with food. That part's right. The chemist was clear on the food.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Omeprazole twenty milligrams once a day, to protect the stomach while you're on the naproxen?
[SEG0039] person_3 (PATIENT): The little capsule, mornings. I take that one properly, every day.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the ibuprofen from before, is that finished?
[SEG0041] person_3 (PATIENT): Stopped. They took me off the ibuprofen when the naproxen started, last year sometime. I don't touch it now.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any allergies I should know about, medicines or otherwise?
[SEG0043] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Nothing. Never had any.
[SEG0044] person_1 (NURSE): I'll slip the cuff on, sit easy. Blood pressure is one thirty-eight over eighty-two, and the pulse is seventy-six.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's a comfortable pressure. May I have a look at the knee?
[SEG0046] person_3 (PATIENT): Fire ahead. Left one, like I said.
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): No redness. It's not warm. I can't see any swelling. There is a creak when you bend it, though. And again... grand, that's enough.
[SEG0048] person_3 (PATIENT): A creak. Sure the garden gate creaks and nobody x-rays the gate.

[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): The creak fits wear and tear, but I still won't pick a single cause. Osteoarthritis or bursitis, either is possible. An x-ray this morning wouldn't change what we do, so I won't pretend otherwise.
[SEG0050] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He was on the buildings for years, retired now. Lives on his own. I come weekday mornings, around nine, and I leave a dinner some days.
[SEG0051] person_3 (PATIENT): You can skip the life story. I gave up the cigarettes ten years ago. I might have a pint of a weekend, maybe. Hardly worth the ink.
[SEG0052] person_2 (DOCTOR): The cigarettes long stopped, I'll note that. Any falls in the last while?
[SEG0053] person_3 (PATIENT): No falls. I'm not doddery.
[SEG0054] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the rest of you. Chest, breathing, waterworks, anything playing up?
[SEG0055] person_3 (PATIENT): All quiet. Not a bother on that side of things.

[SEG0056] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. With the ramipril and the anti-inflammatory together, I'd like a kidney blood test today. I'm not saying there's a kidney problem. Let's see what the tests say, and nothing more than that.
[SEG0057] person_1 (NURSE): I can take urea and electrolytes after ye finish, if you want it on today's card.
[SEG0058] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes please, today. And if the knee isn't settling when I see you again, we might arrange an x-ray then. I'm not booking one now.
[SEG0059] person_3 (PATIENT): And the script itself? That's the whole reason I came down.

[SEG0060] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll renew what you're already taking. Nothing stronger gets added. Ramipril, the statin, omeprazole, paracetamol, and naproxen once we actually know the strength in the box.
[SEG0061] person_2 (DOCTOR): Bring that naproxen box next time. Don't double it up on a bad day. Little walks are better than none, and a bit of ice if you've been on the leg. No heroics.
[SEG0062] person_3 (PATIENT): Ice, walks, no extra tablets. Very ordinary, for all the fuss.
[SEG0063] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Ordinary will do. I'll put the box in the bag tonight so we're not hunting for it.
[SEG0064] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll see you in three months for the repeats, and we'll settle the naproxen dose properly then.
[SEG0065] person_3 (PATIENT): Three months. If I'm worse I might show up, I suppose. I probably won't be.
[SEG0066] person_2 (DOCTOR): If the knee swells or you can't walk on it, come back sooner. Don't sit on it for the three months.
[SEG0067] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'll have him down if that happens. Thanks for taking the time.
[SEG0068] person_1 (NURSE): Bloods are just down the hall when you're ready, and the script will be at reception.
[SEG0069] person_3 (PATIENT): Grand so. Let's get the needle done. Desperate day out there anyway, I'd no business on the lane.
[SEG0070] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mind yourself on the step. Take care now.

spec.situation: Routine repeat-prescription review at a small clinic with a pharmacy technician present; patient wants a stronger painkiller; tablet names and doses are discussed in detail, one dose is read from the pharmacy list and differs from the patient's own; doctor declines the stronger medicine.
features: ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.

doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.
disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.

third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.
